Assumptions

Switching from CHP to heat pump cuts energy cost by 65 % and CO2 by 76 %.The constraint is winter grid supply, not economics.

Timeline.

The heat pump is the more economical and lower-emission heat source.But grid draw rises 36-fold over the year.

The heat pump reduces energy cost by 65 % and CO2 by 76 % versus the CHP.In return, grid draw rises from 0.4 to 13.6 MWh a year.

Model and assumptions.

For reference.

The model.493 single optimisations of 48 hours each, re-planned every 24 h, per scenario.

Balances, every hour

PV − curtailed + CHP + grid draw + battery out = household + EV + heat pump + heater + battery in + feed-in
grid draw and feed-in never in the same hour; battery in and out never in the same hour; no battery out in a feed-in hour
buffer(t) = 0.99 · buffer(t−1) + heat pump + CHP + heater − space heat − hot water from buffer
hot water = heat pump at hot-water COP, or CHP / heater in the same hour

Scenarios

1 · Financial optimumgrid draw × retail price + gas + maintenance + starts + battery wear − PV and CHP revenue
2 · Lowest CO2 emissionsgrid draw × hourly grid intensity + gas × 201 g/kWh
3 · Maximum autarkyelectricity drawn from the grid
4 · Maximum self-consumptionfeed-in + curtailed PV

Noticed in the data

    Every figure on this site is computed hour by hour from the measured 2025 data.This page shows each step, the assumption behind it and a worked example.

    Calculation chain.Ten steps from the HEMS export to the charts.

    All worked examples follow one hour: 14 January 2025, 07:00, at −8.9 °C. It is row 321 in every sheet of the Excel file. The examples use the task values (0.27 €/kWh electricity, 0.09 €/kWh gas); the controls on the left do not change this page.

    1 · Input data.Hourly HEMS export, evaluated for the calendar year 2025.

    The export runs from 1 January 2025 to 8 May 2026 (11,819 hours). Each value is the mean power over one hour in kW, which equals the energy of that hour in kWh. 2025 is the only complete year and is used for all annual figures. It has 8,759 hours because one hour is missing at the clock change.

    The CHP column is not modelled: its electricity, heat, battery and grid flows are taken directly from the measurements.

    Example hour: measured values

    CHP electricity6.87 kWh'Input (CHP measured)'!I321
    CHP heat22.59 kWh'Input (CHP measured)'!J321
    PV generation0.00 kWh'Input (CHP measured)'!D321
    House electricity use1.59 kWh'Input (CHP measured)'!L321
    Grid feed-in5.22 kWh'Input (CHP measured)'!G321

    2 · Weekly heat demand.The CHP heat minus hot water and system losses.

    The CHP heat cannot be used hour by hour: the CHP runs on and off into a buffer tank (293 runs in 2025), so its output in one hour is not the demand of that hour. Over a week the buffer evens out, so the balance is done per week.

    • Hot water: 200 litres per day heated by 30 K (owner).
    • On warm days (daily mean above 17 °C) there is no space heating, so the CHP heat on those days is hot water plus losses.
    • The losses (buffer, pipes, cycling) are not carried over to the heat pump (owner).
    Hot water per day = 200 l × 4.186 kJ/(kg·K) × 30 K ÷ 3,600 = 6.98 kWh
    Baseline = mean CHP heat on days above 17 °C = 48.04 kWh per day
    Losses = 48.04 − 6.98 = 41.06 kWh per day
    Space heat of a week = CHP heat of the week − 48.04 × days

    Example: week from 13 January 2025

    CalculationResultExcel
    CHP heat in the weeksum of 168 hours2,974 kWhWeekly!C4
    Hot water + losses48.04 × 7 days336 kWhWeekly!E4
    Space heat of the week2,974 − 3362,638 kWhWeekly!G4

    Baseline from sheet Daily, all days in the data set with a daily mean above 17 °C (Parameter!C12). Hot water: Parameter!C9–C11.

    3 · From week to hour.Colder hours get a larger share of the weekly heat.

    Each hour gets heating degree hours: how many degrees it was below the heating limit of 17 °C. The weekly space heat is split in proportion to them. Hot water is spread evenly: one 24th of 6.98 kWh every hour.

    Result for 2025: the heat pump has to supply 60,526 kWh of heat, against 74,984 kWh measured at the CHP.

    Heating degree hours = max(0, 17 °C − outside temperature)
    Space heat of the hour = space heat of the week × degree hours of the hour ÷ degree hours of the week

    Example hour

    CalculationResultExcel
    Heating degree hours17 − (−8.9)25.9 K·h'HP calculation'!I321
    Degree hours of the weeksum of 168 hours3,276 K·hWeekly!F4

    Hot water6.98 ÷ 240.29 kWh'HP calculation'!K321
    Heat needed this hour20.85 + 0.2921.14 kWh'Output (HP, no CHP)'!Q321

    4 · Heating curve.The colder it is outside, the hotter the heating water has to be.

    The owner's heating curve gives three points: 45 °C flow at −20 °C, 35 °C at 0 °C and 25 °C at +20 °C. In between the flow temperature is a straight line: half a degree warmer water per degree colder air. Hot water always needs 55 °C.

    Flow temperature = 35 °C − 0.5 × outside temperature

    Example hour

    CalculationResultExcel
    Flow temperature35 − 0.5 × (−8.9)39.45 °C'HP calculation'!C321

    Heating curve points: Parameter!C3–C8.

    5 · COP.Outside temperature × flow temperature, both interpolated from the datasheet.

    The datasheet gives the COP at six outside temperatures, each for 35 °C and for 55 °C water. The COP of an hour is found in two steps:

    • Between the two neighbouring outside temperatures, for both water temperatures.
    • Between 35 °C and 55 °C, at the flow temperature of the hour (owner: linear relation). Below 35 °C the line is extended. Below −15 °C the −15 °C values are used.

    Datasheet values (Lambda EU20L)

    OutsideCOP at 35 °CCOP at 55 °C
    −15 °C3.102.47
    −10 °C3.442.59
    −7 °C3.852.72
    +2 °C5.654.46
    +7 °C6.595.48
    +12 °C8.677.54
    COP = COP35 + (flow − 35) ÷ 20 × (COP55 − COP35)

    Example hour: −8.9 °C outside, 39.45 °C flow

    CalculationResultExcel
    COP at 35 °C water3.44 + (1.1 ÷ 3) × (3.85 − 3.44)3.59'HP calculation'!P321
    COP at 55 °C water2.59 + (1.1 ÷ 3) × (2.72 − 2.59)2.64'HP calculation'!Q321
    COP space heating3.59 + (39.45 − 35) ÷ 20 × (2.64 − 3.59)3.38'HP calculation'!D321
    COP hot waterCOP at 55 °C2.64'HP calculation'!R321

    1.1 ÷ 3: −8.9 °C lies 1.1 K above −10 °C, within the 3 K step to −7 °C. Source: the owner's curve file, sheet Annahmen; in the Excel sheet Kennlinie.

    6 · Power limit and immersion heater.Above 20 kW the heat pump needs electric backup.

    The heat pump delivers at most 20 kW of heat above −10 °C and 17.9 kW at −15 °C, linear in between (datasheet). It covers space heating first, then hot water. Anything above the limit comes from the immersion heater, which turns 1 kWh of electricity into 1 kWh of heat (COP 1).

    In 2025 this happens in 110 hours on 18 days, 175 kWh in total. Without a buffer tank in the model this is an upper bound.

    Immersion heater = heat needed − heat-pump maximum (if positive)

    Example hour

    CalculationResultExcel
    Heat-pump maximum−8.9 °C is above −10 °C20.00 kW'HP calculation'!L321
    Heat pump, space heatingmin(20.85, 20)20.00 kWh'HP calculation'!M321
    Heat pump, hot watermin(0.29, 20 − 20)0.00 kWh'HP calculation'!N321
    Immersion heater21.14 − 201.14 kWh'HP calculation'!O321

    Limits: Parameter!C19–C21.

    7 · Heat-pump electricity.Heat divided by its COP, for each part separately.

    Over the year the heat pump uses 11,165 kWh of electricity for 60,526 kWh of heat. That is a seasonal performance factor (SPF) of 5.42.

    Electricity = space heat ÷ COP + hot water ÷ COP55 + immersion heater

    Example hour

    CalculationResultExcel
    Space heating20.00 ÷ 3.385.92 kWh
    Hot water0.00 ÷ 2.640.00 kWh
    Immersion heater1.14 ÷ 11.14 kWh
    Heat-pump electricity5.92 + 0 + 1.147.06 kWh'HP calculation'!E321
    SPF 202560,526 ÷ 11,1655.42Comparison!D12

    8 · Battery and grid.The owner's rules, applied hour by hour in sequence.

    • The house load is the measured use (incl. wallbox) plus the heat-pump electricity.
    • PV covers the load first.
    • A surplus charges the battery (39.5 kWh, max. 20 kW); the rest is fed into the grid.
    • A deficit is taken from the battery; the rest comes from the grid.

    The battery is lossless (the owner gives no losses) and starts at 93.3 %. Its charge carries over from one hour to the next, so this step has to run in time order.

    Balance = PV − (house use + heat-pump electricity)

    Example 1: 14 January 2025, 07:00 (deficit)

    9 · Gas, cost and CO2.Hourly energy flows times prices and emission factors, summed over the year.

    Gas is not metered. It is derived from the CHP output with an overall efficiency of 0.85 on the gross calorific value (our assumption; 0.80–0.90 gives 108–122 MWh). Feed-in earns nothing in the base case. The CO2 factor of grid electricity is the German annual mean 2024.

    Gas = (CHP electricity + CHP heat) ÷ 0.85
    Cost = gas × 0.09 €/kWh + grid draw × 0.27 €/kWh − feed-in × 0 €/kWh
    CO2 = gas × 0.181 kg/kWh + grid draw × 0.363 kg/kWh

    Example hour

    CHPHeat pump
    Gas(6.87 + 22.59) ÷ 0.85 = 34.66 kWh0 kWh
    Grid draw0 kWh8.65 kWh
    Cost34.66 × 0.09 = 3.12 €8.65 × 0.27 = 2.34 €
    CO234.66 × 0.181 = 6.27 kg8.65 × 0.363 = 3.14 kg

    Limitations.What the model leaves out, and in which direction it errs.

    SimplificationEffect on the result
    No buffer tank in the heat-pump modelImmersion heater and winter peaks are an upper bound
    Datasheet COP without defrosting and pumpsHeat-pump electricity rather too low; a 15 % lower COP reduces the saving by about 0.5 k€ per year
    Lossless batteryGrid draw slightly too low
    Annual mean CO2 factorWinter grid electricity is dirtier than average, so heat-pump CO2 is rather too low
    Heat demand shaped by outside temperature onlyNo sun, wind or occupancy effects within a week; weekly totals stay correct
    Hourly resolutionPeaks shorter than one hour are not visible
    Gas derived, not meteredCHP cost and CO2 ±6 % for an efficiency of 0.80–0.90
